The tornado formed 4 miles east of Alba in a location on Olds Rd 0.5 miles east of the Alba Rd intersection. It tracked east northeast for about 1.75 miles before exiting Antrim county 200 yards southeast of the Alba Rd/Old Alba Rd intersection. The tornado continued in Otsego county for almost 16 additional miles before dissipating at 1457 EST. In Antrim county, no injuries or fatalities were reported. Several homes were damaged along with numerous softwood trees snapped at their trunks (DI 28, DOD 4) along Patterson Rd. While the highest rating of EF1 in Antrim county was assigned at this location, the tornado was rated EF3 in Otsego county. The maximum path width in Antrim county was 200 yards.

This tornado formed in Antrim county 4 miles east of Alba and continued into Otsego county 100 yards SE of the Alba Rd/Old Alba Rd intersection. The tornado continued to move east northeast for almost 16 additional miles before dissipating around 1.75 miles northeast of Sparr. The tornado was rated EF3 in Otsego county based on damage surveyed in multiple locations around the Gaylord area. The first of these locations was damage in the Nottingham Forest manufactured home community. Multiple units were completely destroyed with debris blown away from the original locations of the units (DI 4, DOD 12). The second location was the business district of Gaylord where the buildings of Hobby Lobby, Maurices, and Jimmy Johns experienced collapses of exterior walls where interior walls remained standing (DI 10, DOD 8). The last location, which had the highest estimated wind speed of 150 mph, was damage found to homes on Berkshire Ln on the northeast side of Gaylord. Most exterior walls were collapsed and only partial interior walls were left standing (DI 2, DOD 8).  The tornado dissipated at 1457 EST about 1.75 miles northeast of Sparr. Two fatalities were reported in the Nottingham Forest community, along with 44 injuries reported from various locations around Gaylord. The maximum path width in Otsego county was 200 yards.

High snow-to-liquid ratios and intense, generally persistent bands with consistent 1 inch per hour snowfall rates resulted in the accumulation of 24.8 inches of snow by midnight on the 30th...setting a new calendar day record for the Gaylord area. Most intense snowfall occurred on the 29th into the morning of the 30th, with much less impressive snowfall rates for the remainder of the weekend in the immediate area of the office...with a 60-hr snowfall total of 33.8 inches ending 1900EST on the 30th. Highest snow depth during this period was 21 inches on the 30th...with an event total of 45.4inches by 1900EST December 2nd. Travel impacts were somewhat widespread, particularly focused beneath the snow bands, where whiteout conditions and significant snow accumulations on roadways made travel difficult to nearly impossible. Large tree blown down onto home, and a roof blown off a campground building, amid other wind damage reports from the East Jordan area. Trained spotter reported a gust to 52 mph in the Boyne City area, and the AWOS sensor at the Boyne Falls airport reported a gust to 51mph at 21:34. Several power outages were noted in the East Jordan area during the evening and overnight, prior to icing-related outages.

Significant icing across the county, particularly north and west of Harrisville, resulting in numerous downed trees and powerlines, as well as gas shortages. Radial ice measurements around 5/8 inch in Curran in eastern Alcona county, according to amateur radio operators/volunteer fire.

In excess of one-half inch of radial ice accumulation was measured near Lachine. Widespread ice damage countywide, to trees and power/communications infrastructure, with nearly 100 percent of Alpena county without power at the peak of the storm. Alpena Power Company lost all power after the substation serving their grid went down for close to 2 days. The ASOS at the Alpena County Regional Airport, due to power outages, was unable to report critical weather/historical weather information for almost 6 days, between March 29th and April 4th. Some farmers ran generators part time between their homes and their barns to keep livestock safe. An Alpena Public Schools agriscience teacher estimated up to 25 percent of students' greenhouse hanging flower baskets were damaged by cold exposure due to lack of power and heat.

Areas of significant tree and infrastructure damage in Antrim county were largely confined to the higher elevations, particularly near the Lakes of the North community in eastern Antrim county, though additional damage was sustained near Atwood in western Antrim County. Estimates of 1/4 to 1/2 inch or more of radial ice accumulation, with highest amounts in the Lakes of the North area.
Significant ice damage to parts of Beaver Island, resulting in the National Guard and Michigan Department of Natural Resources being deployed to Beaver Island for cleanup and restoration efforts.

Widespread radial ice reports of one-half to as much as three-quarters of an inch of ice across parts of the county, with highest amounts near Elmira and Thumb Lake in eastern Charlevoix county, though significant tree and power/communication infrastructure damage was reported across the county. While many areas received ice, including along the coast of Little Traverse Bay north of Charlevoix, lower elevation areas did not receive nearly as much ice or damage from the ice storm.

Up to 93% of electrical customers across all power companies were out of power at the peak of the ice storm. Major roads, including US-23 between Cheboygan and Presque Isle, were closed at times due to downed powerlines and trees. Total ice accumulations well over 1/2 inch.

Widespread power outages and trees down due to significant icing, especially across northern Crawford county. The hospital in Grayling was on generator power. Crawford County issued a request for people to stay home and off the roads due to the ice storm. Thousands of line workers were housed at Camp Grayling during the ice storm in support of clean-up and recovery efforts.

Significant icing across the county, resulting in numerous downed trees and powerlines, as well as gas shortages related to power outages at distribution centers in ice storm affected areas, and frequent and prolonged closures of the Mackinac Bridge due to falling ice concerns. Mackinac Bridge employees reported unprecedented amounts of ice buildup on the Bridge cables and towers following the ice storm, which took several days to finally clear off.

KPLN, Pellston Regional Airport, ASOS reported 1/4 inch of ice accumulation by 2200 LST on the 28th. Closer to Little Traverse Bay, the cooperative observer at North Central Michigan College in Petoskey reported 1/4 inch of radial ice by the morning observation for the 29th; maximum radial ice accumulation at this cooperative observing station was 0.86inch. Other areas of the county received upwards of 3/4 inch of radial ice accumulation, with significant tree and infrastructure damage, including multiple TV and FM radio broadcast towers being toppled due to the weight of the ice.

Significant icing of amounts greater than a quarter inch (radial) resulted in power outages and tree damage on the island; residents were able to ice skate on the streets, though online sales from year-round businesses on the island were impacted by the power outages. Many roads and trails were closed due to tree damage. The National Guard was deployed to Mackinac Island to help with cleanup.

By 8pm EDT on the 29th, enough ice had accreted that Montmorency County emergency management issued a shelter in place notice due to danger posed by falling trees. Multiple shelters were set up across the county, with local businesses stepping up to help their communities while power companies worked tirelessly to rebuild much of the power and communication infrastructure in the county, destroyed due to the weight of ice and falling trees. Over 90% of people in Montmorency county were without power at the peak of the event. Johannesburg-Lewiston School District was closed for 2 weeks due to the ice storm; returning students remained out of power at home for longer. Significant tree damage noted across the county, including destruction of maple trees and equipment used in the production of maple syrup.

Significant icing across the county, particularly northwestern Oscoda county, resulting in widespread tree and power/communication infrastructure damage. Multiple warming shelters opened. Amateur radio/volunteer fire in the Mio area reported 5/8 inch of ice.

Widespread radial ice reports of one-half to as much as three-quarters of an inch of ice across the county, with highest amounts in the Gaylord and Elmira areas. Significant damage to trees and property, including homes. Extensive damage to power and communication infrastructure, with power outages lasting multiple weeks, into late April. NWS Gaylord employees, unable to make it home due to trees and powerlines blocking roads, slept over at the office for multiple days; the office was on generator power from Saturday through the following Thursday.

Trained spotter measured upwards of three-quarters of an inch of radial ice accretion at a home right on the Lake Huron coast. Spotter also reported extensive damage to trees and power/communications infrastructure throughout the county, with nearly complete business closures, largely due to significant and widespread power outages. The primary local electric cooperative serving Presque Isle county reported their entire system had been knocked offline for the first time in history.

Significant icing around or greater than 1/4 inch (radial) across the county, resulting in numerous downed trees and powerlines, as well as gas shortages related to power outages at distribution centers in ice storm affected areas. Warming shelters were opened in Engadine.

Significant water level changes measured by water level equipment at the Point Iroquois, MI Light on the southern shore of Whitefish Bay as a mesolow at the heart of a decaying line of storms crossed the lake. A 3.75-ft change in water level from trough to peak during the morning hours is the largest in 30-years of water level records at Point Iroquois, MI. Water level fluctuations of 18 or more inches continued through the next day; elevated seiche activity was observed in the Whitefish Bay basin through the next several days.

Significant water level changes measured by water level equipment at Southwest Pier at the mouth of the St. Mary's River shipping channel, upstream of the Soo Locks. An amplitude of 6.67-ft of change from trough to peak is the largest in 20 years of seiche/meteotsunami data at this location. This resulted in delay of marine traffic through the Soo Locks until water level fluctuations had dampened enough for safe navigation of the shipping channel on the upstream end of the Soo Locks. Water level fluctuations were also noted on the Sault Ste. Marie, MI power canal, resulting in impacts to the Cloverland Hydroelectric Plant at the end of the power canal downstream of the Soo Locks. Additional periodic water level fluctuations were noted around Whitefish Bay and the upper St. Mary's River for the next several days until finally settling back down to normal.

An extremely photogenic tornadic waterspout developed over central Torch Lake and dissipated shortly after making landfall on the eastern shore of Torch Lake north of the mouth of the Clam River. Only minor tree damage was observed. Event was initially reported to NWS Gaylord by a storm chaser watching a Torch Lake area webcam; chaser reported seeing debris lofted in the air on the webcam footage as the waterspout made landfall.

The tip of the Leelanau Peninsula near Northport received as much as 9 inches of snow as early as mid-morning, thanks to off-shore band just barely nicking the tip of the peninsula. As the band moved inland, additional snow fell, with reports of as much as 10 inches at Stony Point, northeast of Suttons Bay on the east side of the Leelanau Peninsula.  Snow to liquid ratios were as high as 20 to 1.

As much as 9.5 inches of snow fell over parts of west-central Grand Traverse county thanks to passage of a mesovortex during the early afternoon, followed by north-northeasterly flow lake effect in the late afternoon and evening hours on the 9th.

Twenty-four hour snowfall total between midnight on the 27th and 28th at WFO Gaylord, 9mi SSW of the city of Gaylord, MI, was 13.1 inches, with a storm total of 19.6 inches. Areas just west and south of the office, particularly the Wilderness Valley and Waters area were more consistently beneath the more intense snow band, received nearly 20 inches of snow by the middle of the day on the 27th...with storm totals as high as 25inches. Snowfall totals varied dramatically across the county, with some areas (not under the band) receiving closer to 10 inches or less over the course of 72 hrs.

Storm total snowfall near Mancelona of 18.4 inches by the morning of the 29th. Snowfall totals in parts of Antrim county as high as 20 inches in the vicinity of Alba and parts of Lakes of the North...though some areas even 10 miles away from the CoCoRaHS observer only received a couple inches for the entire event.

Snowfall amounts varied dramatically across the county depending on which areas were and were not under the band. Areas closer to the town of Kalkaska proper, well away from the most intense band, received closer to 3-4 inches of snow, while areas across northeastern portion of the county received at least 2 feet of snow. Highest report was 25.5 inches in Blue Lake Township by the middle of the day on the 28th.

Snowfall totals by mid-morning on the 27th were as high as 20 inches. Highest storm total snowfall report near May Lake, southwest of the town of Frederic, was 23.3 inches. Reports continued to vary across the county depending on where the most intense band stayed persistent longest; areas closer to Lovells, only 15miles ENE of May Lake, reported a storm total of 11.5 inches. The cooperative observer in Grayling, MI measured a total of 17 inches by the morning of the 29th. NWS employee traveling south on Old 27 between Waters and Grayling during the morning of the 27th estimated at least 14 inches on the ground and whiteout conditions near Frederic.
Snowfall totals in the East Jordan area of 7-12 inches.

Localized snowfall totals of 7-9 inches over 48-72 hours, generally over parts of eastern Grand Traverse county, downstream of Grand Traverse Bay. Some parts of the county saw less than 4 inches through the event.

Upwards of 12-16 inches of snow had fallen across western Chippewa County by the morning of the 29th. Strong winds led to significant blowing and drifting of snow, to the extent road commissions struggled to keep roads clear. This resulted in the Chippewa County Road Commission issuing a statement on social media urging residents to stay home unless absolutely necessary. Final snowfall totals as high as 20-24inches. Air traffic at Alpena Regional Airport was suspended due to ice. Additional reports of up to 0.25 inches of radial ice accumulation by 0830am on the 11th.

Flat ice accretion reached 0.25 inches between 2100 and 2300 with the bulk of this occurring between 2200 and 2300; an additional 0.10 of flat ice accretion was reported by midday, bringing the storm total flat ice accretion to 0.35, ending 1400 on the 11th. The NWS Gaylord, MI forecast office measured nearly 0.40 of flat ice by 1300 with radial ice accumulation on tree limbs up to 0.20.

Marie during the near-blizzard conditions, but all parties, including the horse, were uninjured.

On Bois Blanc Island, road crews, including a large front-end loader, periodically became stuck in the snow while clearing roads. A man was rescued off the ice near Mackinac Island during whiteout conditions, requiring first responders to venture onto the ice. The half-mile walk back to the shore after the rescue during these conditions took 40 minutes.

Mackinac Bridge was closed for winds and whiteout conditions, and county and state offices were proactively closed for the 16th, with a travel warning issued by emergency management on the evening of the 15th. Snowfall totals as high as 28 inches at DeTour Village, with reports of as much as 34 inches on Drummond Island.

Near-blizzard conditions reported at Pellston Regional Airport, KPLN, on the 15th. At the Fife Lake cooperative observing station, the better portion of the storm total 8.2 inches was sleet. Nearly 0.2 of freezing rain accretion was observed across southwestern portions of the county, along with some tree damage. Traverse City Cherry Capital Airport was closed for 48-hrs due to storm conditions, despite crews working around the clock on the 15th and 16th to keep runways clear. County authorities issued a public safety advisory to residents to stay home during the evening of the 16th due to extremely poor travel conditions.

Total snow and sleet for the event was 13-21 inches, with higest snowfall totals across the northern portion of the county. Storm total at WFO Gaylord, MI, 9 mi SSW of the city of Gaylord, was 13.2 inches, several of which fell as sleet, with less than a tenth of ice accretion overall. On top of regularly scheduled forecasters, three NWS employees -- two forecasters and the Electronics System Analyst -- stayed and slept at the office on the night of the 15th to ensure continuous 24-hour operations during and after the winter storm. The thick, dense snow/sleet pack resulted in significant travel delays on the 16th as crews worked to clear roadways during the day...before additional snow and whiteout conditions resulted in poor travel again on the evening of the 16th.

Storm total snowfall around 20-30 inches across the county, with a few inches of sleet, and a couple tenths of freezing rain reported, especially across the eastern/southeastern half of the county...upwards of three-tenths of an inch or more of ice accretion reported near the town of Presque Isle. Some county offices and the courthouse were closed through the 17th due to the storm and resultant clean up.

Around 60 percent of utility customers were without power in the county by the morning of the 16th.

The Meridian Boundary Fire began as a debris fire that rapidly expanded out of control.  The fire was first spotted at 130 pm on May 18th, and grew very rapidly.  8800 acres would eventually burn, and by May 26th the fire was 95 percent contained.  The fire occurred in southeast Crawford County, contained by Meridian Rd to the east, Pioneer Rd to the south, Willows Rd to the west, and USFS 4209 to the north.  Twelve residences were destroyed, and another six were damaged, and 36 outbuildings were damaged or destroyed.

The Range 9 Fire started on the 18th as a controlled burn on an artillery range on Camp Grayling, a National Guard facility.  The fire got out of control after 230 pm as winds picked up.  Most of the 1100 acres burned were grassy areas on the Camp Grayling grounds.  However, a portion of the fire crossed the military installation's property line near the Manistee River in Blue Lake Township, destroying four seasonal homes.  The fire was under control by late evening.

events.event_narrative: Trees were knocked down in nearby Manistee.
Trees were downed by damaging winds.

These were the largest known hailstones in northern lower Michigan history. Hail reached just slightly larger than softballs, a few miles north of West Branch. Immense property destruction resulted, with many, many vehicles considered to be total losses, and roofs and siding dented and damaged. Around 350 structures were damaged in some way, shape, or form.
Trees were downed on Wright and Lake Streets in Cadillac.

An NWS storm survey team estimated winds in excess of 80 mph crossing much of southern Leelanau County. Thousands of trees were downed in this swath, from the Sleeping Bear Dunes to Grand Traverse Bay. Many homes and vehicles were damaged by falling trees. Area roads were closed for days, in some cases weeks. Glen Arbor was inaccessible via road for two days, until M-22 could be cleared of trees and reopened. The county established drop points for residents to leave storm debris; these remained open for seven weeks after the storm. Across Leelanau County, two homes were destroyed, and over 700 were damaged in some way.
Trees and power lines were downed in northern Leelanau County, though the damage was not as extensive as further south. Still, multiple vehicles and homes were damaged by falling trees.

Considerable wind damage occurred in central Grand Traverse County, including near and just south of Traverse City. Many trees were downed, causing damage to vehicles and homes. Some roads were difficult to travel for a day or two after the storm.

The most concentrated damage in Grand Traverse County occurred on the Old Mission Peninsula. Many trees were down, and multiple vineyards and orchards suffered substantial damage. Vehicles and buildings were also damaged by felled trees. Across Grand Traverse County, nine buildings were considered destroyed, and nearly 400 were damaged in some way.

Considerable wind damage occurred in southwest and south central Antrim County. Many hundreds of trees were downed in these areas, with some resulting in damage to vehicles and structures. Some side streets were difficult to access for a day or two after the storm. Between 40 and 50 structures suffered some amount of damage from the storm.

A swath of widespread wind damage continued across northern Kalkaska County. Hundreds of trees were downed, damaging vehicles and structures as they fell. Between 40 and 50 structures were believed damaged to some extent in Kalkaska County.

The swath of damaging winds continued from further west, but damage was becoming less widespread and more spotty with time. Still, there were occasional pockets were dozens of trees were downed, especially from Frederic to near Grayling. Tress took down power lines, and damaged cars, homes, and businesses. Almost 100 buildings suffered some degree of damage due to the storm.

events.event_narrative: Seven waterspouts were observed off of Charlevoix over a one-hour period.
Peninsula Drive was closed between McKinley and Wilson Roads due to coastal flooding and beach erosion. The east end of Marina Drive in Traverse City was also closed.
The parking lot of the Grand Traverse Yacht Club was flooded.

Flooding covered a portion of Lakeshore Drive at 5th Avenue Beach in Manistee. In Parkdale Township, the beach eroded up to the foundation of several homes, and a number of trees were washed into the lake.
Severe beach erosion threatened to destroy a home several miles north of Frankfort.

In Northport on the 21st, a dock was damaged and a boat house was flooded. Water levels rose over the docks at Northport Marina. On the 22nd in Empire, a part of the break wall at Empire Beach was destroyed. In Glen Haven, restoration efforts from flooding earlier in the month were eliminated, and shoreline fences were destroyed at Glen Haven Beach.
A portion of M-185 on Mackinac Island was washed out.
A dock, boardwalk, and beach signage were destroyed in Parkdale Township.

Extended period of flooding reported. Between Tawas City and Alabaster, dock planks and some trees were washed away. An estimated 20 feet of beach disappeared. The road leading to the lighthouse at Tawas Point State Park was flooded, and eventually covered in sand and rocks.
Just west of Bayshore, a portion of the Little Traverse Wheelway Bike Path was destroyed.
A bike path in Alpena was flooded and covered in sand.
A parking lot next to Betsie Lake in Frankfort flooded. A large field of debris, including entire trees and large tree limbs, was deposited along the beach at Point Betsie Lighthouse.
On the Old Mission Peninsula, docks were washed out. Waves reached the parking lot at Haserot Beach.
Severe beach erosion occurred at Black River. The overlook at the end of East Main Street in Harrisville was damaged.
The Cedar River rose out of its banks, producing minor flooding in Gladwin City Park.
A culvert was washed out along 20 Mile Road near Kelden.

Munson Hospital measured 3.12 inches of rain during the day on the 28th. Most of this was dumped in a short period of time, early in the afternoon. This resulted in a small area of flash flooding, in downtown Traverse City and on the near west side. Water rose up to three feet high on some roads and parking lots, and in a few spots the water was higher. Some people were trapped in vehicles and required rescue. Numerous vehicles were heavily damaged. The basement of Munson Hospital flooded. Kids Creek rose out of banks, flooding roads and some buildings.

Widespread areal flooding developed on the 18th, and persisted for several days. Most creeks and rivers in Gladwin County rose out of their banks. Several hundred miles of roads across the county were closed at various times. The Tobacco River at Beaverton rose to a record crest of 14.32 feet on the morning of the 19th. Somewhat more than 100 residents were evacuated from their homes, including people living below the Chappel Dam on the Cedar River. The M-30 bridge across the Tobacco River where it enters Wixom Lake was destroyed.

Widespread areal flooding developed on the 18th, and persisted for several days. Most creeks and rivers in Arenac County rose out of their banks. Many roads across the county were closed at various times, including M-13 south of Standish. The Rifle River near Sterling reached a new record flood stage of 15.65 feet on the afternoon of the 19th. Some structures along the River River and Parmalee Creek were partially submerged. The Forest Lake area was evacuated due to rising water. Hundreds of homes were flooded in the Standish area. Flooding along the Lake Huron coastline was worsened by lakeshore flooding thanks to onshore winds.

Widespread areal flooding developed in central and southern Iosco County on the 18th. Many creeks and rivers rose out of their banks, including the Au Gres River system and Silver Creek and its tributaries. Many roads across the county were closed, including Meadow Road in Tawas City. Railroad tracks were also washed out in Tawas City. Townline Road in Tawas Township was washed out by Dead Creek. Flooding along the Lake Huron coastline was worsened by lakeshore flooding thanks to onshore winds.

Widespread areal flooding developed in central and southern Ogemaw County on the 18th. Many creeks and rivers rose out of their banks, including the Rifle River system. Many roads across the county were closed. The Prescott area was especially hard hit, with some property damage due to flooding.

Areal flooding developed in central and southeast Roscommon County on the 18th. Some creeks and rivers rose out of their banks. Many roads across the county were impacted by high water, and that included a few closures. There was some property damage due to flooding, especially in parts of Houghton Lake.

Multiple dams on the Tittabawassee River system were in danger during and after the heavy rain event. Significant releases of water from Secord and Smallwood Dams caused periods of rapid, flash flooding downstream of those dams on parts of the 18th and 19th. Tremendous erosion of the river banks occurred, and some roads and properties were damaged. Those releases did manage to save those two dams. However, downstream, Edenville Dam was unable to be saved. That dam failed catastrophically on the evening of the 19th, releasing the contents of Wixom Lake to downstream portions of the Tittabawassee River.|Note that Edenville Dam was located just north of the Gladwin/Midland County line. The Tittabawassee River enters Midland County immediately after leaving the dam. Thus, the vast majority of the downstream flooding caused by the failure of Edenville Dam will be found in Midland County and other downstream counties. Also note that the indirect damages of the Edenville Dam failure in Gladwin County are considerable, but difficult to quantify. To just touch on one topic, there were hundreds of lakefront properties on Wixom Lake, behind the dam. That lake no longer exists, and those properties have seen loss of property value, and residents and vacationers see a lesser quality of life.

Training thunderstorms brought heavy rain to parts of Traverse City. Munson Hospital measured 2.45 of rain during the afternoon and evening. Quick-hitting flash flooding developed in the area, and in particular on the near west side of the city. Kids Creek overflowed its banks. Cedar Street and other roads near Munson Hospital were flooded. This event was extremely similar, though not quite as hard hitting, as the flash flood event in the same location back on May 28 2020.
